group receives BPA administration, anesthesia, and prolonged beam irradiation, whereas the X-ray
group does not include these elements and their effect on the immune response cannot be ruled out.
Sham administration and anesthesia procedures must also be applied to the x-ray group.
- We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. BPA administration is an integral part
of BNCT treatment, and therefore comparing BNCT with X-ray under these conditions necessarily
involves its use. Importantly, the safety of BPA has been extensively studied, based on those applied
in preclinical and clinical BNCT studies12-15, at the concentrations used in our experiments, it does
not induce immune responses. In addition, to ensure immobilization and precise tumour targeting,
mice in the X-ray group were also anesthetized and sham administration during irradiation, and the
anesthesia procedure was consistent between BNCT and X-ray groups. We have clarified this point
in the revised manuscript to avoid potential misunderstanding.
3) Cells derived from 3 mice in each group were pooled for analysis and may be considered n=1 for
statistical purposes. Independence of statistical analysis is not ensured and generalization of results
requires careful interpretation.
- We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this critical point regarding the statistical independence
of our scRNA-seq samples.
First, pooling cells from multiple animals into a single sequencing library was implemented to
minimize technical batch effects, which is a major concern during our experimental design.
Processing each mouse individually could introduce substantial technical variation that might obscure
the biological signals of interest. This approach is well-established in the field; for instance, in a
seminal study in scRNA-seq field (Cell, 2015, “Highly Parallel Genome-wide Expression Profiling
of Individual Cells Using Nanoliter Droplets”16), researchers mixed 44,808 cells from four samples
and then successfully identified both known neuronal classes and novel cell types.
Second, in scRNA-seq protocols, each cell undergoes independent RNA extraction, library
preparation, and sequencing. Therefore, each cell can be treated as an independent observational
unit—analogous to a sample in bulk RNA-seq. This practice is widespread and supported by
numerous high-impact studies. Examples include the original SMART-seq protocol paper (Nature
Biotechnology, 2012, “Full-length mRNA-Seq from single-cell levels of RNA and individual
circulating tumour cells”17), a scRNA-seq atlas of colorectal cancer (Cell, 2021, “Spatially organized
multicellular immune hubs in human colorectal cancer”18), and, a pan-cancer T cell atlas study
(Nature Medicine, 2023, “Pan-cancer T cell atlas links a cellular stress response state to
immunotherapy resistance”19), among many others.
Lastly, key findings from our scRNA-seq analysis were experimentally validated. For example, in
Fig. 5, we observed elevated antigen processing and presentation activity in DCs following BNCT
treatment. This was corroborated by flow cytometry, which confirmed increased expression of the
co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 in DCs from both B16F10 and MC38 tumours after BNCT.
The consistency between computational and experimental results reinforces the reliability of our
scRNA-seq findings.
In summary, pooling cells from multiple biological replicates is a common strategy to reduce batch
effects in scRNA-seq studies pooling cells from multiple biological replicates is a widely adopted
strategy to mitigate batch effects in scRNA-seq studies. Each cell is treated as an independent unit
during statistical analysis—an approach supported by standard analytic protocols. The analytical
results were further validated by their strong concordance with follow-up experimental data.
Collectively, these findings validate the robustness and generalizability of our statistical approach.

5) The analysis time points are not aligned with Day 1/7 for B16F10 and Day 5 for MC38, which
may cause bias in the comparison. The difference in time points needs to be clearly explained.
- We thank the reviewer for pointing out this important consideration. Firstly, the tumour volume
growth rate is different in the two tumour models. Secondly, the response of the two tumours to
BNCT is different. In view of this difference, the time points for analysis were selected based on the
differential radiation sensitivity of the two tumour models (which is the inflection point of the tumour
growth curve as shown). For MC38 tumours, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 1i, tumour volume
peaked on Day 5 after BNCT treatment, which guided our selection of this time point for single-cell
sequencing. In contrast, B16F10 tumours are less sensitive to BNCT, as indicated by both in vitro
and in vivo experiments, so we extended the sampling to Day 7 to better capture treatment effects.
Additionally, to observe dynamic changes following irradiation, we also included samples collected
at Day 1.
6) There is an increase in the percentage of immune cells in the tumour after BNCT treatment, but
this may be a “relative increase” due to a decrease in tumour cells rather than an increase in the
number of immune cells. Absolute count or density data should be presented.
- We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. While we agree that relative percentages of
immune cells may be influenced by the decrease in tumour cells after BNCT, we consider immune
cell proportions to be particularly relevant for understanding the immune landscape during tumour
regression. A higher proportion of immune cells relative to tumour cells indicates the greater the
immune system's numerical advantage over tumour cells, which enhances the potential for tumour
clearance. Even if the absolute density of immune cells is high, their ability to effectively eliminate
tumour cells may be limited if the tumour cell population remains dominant.
To address the reviewer’s concern, we have quantified the absolute number of infiltrating immune
cells. Compared with the control group, BNCT treatment significantly increased the counts of CD8+

with X-ray treatment, BNCT also induced a significant increase in CD11c+ MHC-II+ DCs (Fig.
R18c), which plays the important role in antigen presenting. These results indicated that BNCT not
only alters relative proportions but also increase the absolute infiltration of key immune cell
populations.
